title: Thy first charity (Apocalypse 2:1–7)
hookLine: Ephesus works hard but has left its first love

lines: A HOME RUN LIKE A COMPANY.
cards: They run their home like a well-managed company: a shared calendar, bills paid on time, kids at practice. Nothing is falling apart.
It's just that neither can remember the last time they sat on the porch and simply talked, the way they did when they first met, for hours, about nothing.
After the vision of chapter one, the Apocalypse turns to seven short letters for seven churches. The first goes to Ephesus, a very well-run church.

teach.b: Ephesus was a great city, home to the temple of the goddess the Douay-Rheims calls Diana, Artemis in Greek.
Paul spent years there, the Acts of the Apostles says; Christian tradition says John lived there too, and some traditions add Mary. A church with history. The letter opens with praise.
I know your works, Christ says: your labor, your patience. You can't stand evil. You've tested people who called themselves apostles and found them false.
You've endured for my name and haven't grown weary.

teach.h: THOU HAST LEFT THY FIRST CHARITY.
teach.b: Then the turn, in the Douay-Rheims: "But I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first charity."

teach.h: REMEMBER, REPENT, DO THE FIRST WORKS.
teach.b: First charity: your first love. The works are all there. The love that started them has drifted away, the way a couple can keep a house running and stop really seeing each other.
The remedy comes in three steps. Remember where you fell from. Repent, which the Douay-Rheims calls doing penance.
And do the first works, the things you did when the love was new. Not new strategies. The first things.
The warning is serious: otherwise, he says, I will move your candlestick out of its place. A church can stay busy and still go out like a lamp.

teach.h: THE TREE OF LIFE, OPEN AGAIN.
teach.b: But the letter ends with a promise, as every one of the seven does: to him that overcometh, I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.
The tree from the garden of Eden, closed off since Genesis, opens again at the end of the Bible.

how: Catholics may return to their first love for God through retreats, renewing baptismal promises at Easter, going back to confession, or revisiting the prayers and practices that first drew them into faith.

o: the city in Asia Minor where Paul was born and raised
a great city whose busy church had left its first love
a desert town known for its early monks and hermits

games.q: the letter to Ephesus — tap the pairs.
p: the love that was left behind
will be moved if they don't repent

s: Ephesus is scolded for being lazy
the letter praises their work and patience. what's missing is the first love.
the remedy includes doing the first works again
remember, repent, and do the first works.
every one of the seven letters ends with a promise to the one who overcomes
for Ephesus, it's the tree of life in the paradise of God.

games.q: you're a leader in the church at Ephesus. you work hard, you test false teachers, you haven't grown weary. the letter says you've left your first love. what are you told to do?
o: remember, repent, and do the first works.
games.why: not more effort, not a new plan: go back. remember where you fell from, and do the first works, the things you did when the love was new.

practice: Go back to a time when faith felt alive: a first Communion, a retreat, a moment in an empty church, or simply a time you felt close to God.

If none comes, think of the first time anything stirred your wonder, a night sky, a piece of music, and let it come back in detail. What did you do then that you've stopped doing? If you pray, ask for that first love back.

wordCard.voice: Ephesus, the city. The first of the seven churches addressed in Apocalypse two, praised for its labor but told it had left its first love. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: thy first love (Apocalypse 2:4); the Douay-Rheims, following Latin caritas, says charity.

carryVoice: Your line: the first charity. Busy is not the same as loving. That's day six hundred twenty-one.
